how-much-does-fiverr-take.html.text:
← Upwork vs. Fiverr fee calculator

How much does Fiverr actually take?

Unlike Upwork's fee, this one is short to answer: Fiverr keeps a flat 20% of every order. There are no tiers, no volume discount, and no difference by seller level — a brand-new seller and a Top Rated Seller both pay the same 20%. It applies to the whole order value, including tips and any extras a buyer adds, not just the base package price.

It was not always flat. Before late 2022, Fiverr ran a tiered commission structure that rewarded sellers with more lifetime order volume with a lower cut, reportedly falling toward the 10% range for its highest tiers. Retiring that structure in favor of one flat rate for every seller was a real pay cut for the sellers who had worked their way into a lower tier — worth knowing if an older page or forum post still describes a tiered Fiverr fee as current.

The 20% commission is also not the only figure between an order and your bank account. Fiverr holds order funds in escrow for a clearance period after the order is marked complete — around 14 days for most sellers, shorter for Top Rated Sellers — before they can be withdrawn. Withdrawing to PayPal carries no fee from Fiverr, though PayPal can charge its own currency-conversion fee if your account's default currency differs from the payout currency; withdrawing by bank transfer carries a flat fee of a few dollars per withdrawal. Those are separate from, and on top of, the 20% order commission.

Common questions

What percentage does Fiverr take from sellers in 2026?

A flat 20%. Fiverr keeps 20% of every order's value, with no tiers, no volume discount, and no exception for seller level (New Seller through Top Rated Seller all pay the same rate). The 20% also applies to tips and to any extras added to an order, not just the base package price.

Has Fiverr's seller fee always been flat 20%?

No. Before late 2022, Fiverr ran a tiered commission structure that rewarded sellers with more lifetime volume with a lower cut, reportedly as low as around 10% for its highest tiers. That structure was retired in favor of the single flat 20% every seller pays today, which was a real pay cut for the sellers who had worked their way into a lower tier.

Does Fiverr charge a fee to withdraw earnings?

It depends on the payout method, and it is separate from the 20% order commission. Withdrawing to PayPal carries no Fiverr-side fee, though PayPal itself can charge a currency-conversion fee (commonly a few percent) if your PayPal account's default currency differs from the payout currency. Bank transfer carries a flat fee of a few dollars per withdrawal. Fiverr also holds funds in escrow for a clearance period after an order completes — around 14 days for most sellers, shorter for Top Rated Sellers — before they can be withdrawn at all.

How do I work out what I actually keep from a Fiverr order?

Take the order total (including any tip and extras), subtract Fiverr's flat 20%, then subtract any withdrawal fee for the payout method you use and whatever share you set aside for taxes. how-much-does-upwork-take.html.text:
← Upwork vs. Fiverr fee calculator

How much does Upwork actually take?

Until May 2025, the answer was a table: 20% on the first $500 billed to a client, 10% on the next chunk up to $10,000, and 5% above that, all tracked per client relationship over the contract's lifetime. That table is retired. It is worth knowing it existed, because a lot of pages written before the change still describe it as current.

Since May 1, 2025, Upwork charges a variable freelancer service fee between 0% and 15% per contract. Upwork's own pricing system sets the number for a given client relationship — freelancers with more billing history with a specific client tend to see a lower rate, with well-established relationships able to fall toward 0%, while a new client relationship typically starts near the top of the range. The exact mechanics of how the system picks a number are not fully published.

What is guaranteed: you see the exact percentage before you commit. It is shown when you send a proposal or receive an offer, and it is locked for that contract once work begins — it will not move mid contract, and a different contract, even with the same client, can carry a different quoted rate.

That is also why no calculator — this one included — can tell you your Upwork fee from a formula. There is no formula to run any more. What a calculator can do is take the percentage Upwork already quoted you and turn it into an actual take-home figure, next to withdrawal fees and a tax reserve you set yourself.

Run your quoted fee through the calculator

Common questions

What percentage does Upwork take from freelancers in 2026?

There is no single answer any more. Since May 1, 2025, Upwork replaced its old tiered freelancer service fee (20% on the first $500 billed to a client, 10% up to $10,000, 5% above that) with a variable fee between 0% and 15% per contract. Upwork's own pricing system sets the exact percentage per client relationship, and it is shown to you only when you send a proposal or accept an offer — not published as a table anyone can look up.

Why did Upwork change its fee structure?

Upwork has described the change as rewarding long-term client relationships: freelancers with more billing history with a specific client tend to see a lower fee on that contract, with the rate able to fall toward 0% for well-established relationships, while a brand-new client relationship typically starts near the top of the 0-15% range. The mechanics of exactly how the percentage is set are Upwork's own pricing system and are not fully public.

Is my Upwork fee the same on every contract?

No. The fee is set per contract at the time you send a proposal or receive an offer, and it is locked for that contract's duration once work begins. A different client, or a new contract with the same client, can carry a different quoted percentage.

How do I calculate what I'll actually keep from an Upwork contract?

Look at the percentage Upwork itself quoted you for that specific contract — it is shown before you accept — and use that as the fee in a payout calculator rather than assuming a fixed rate. This site's Upwork vs. Fiverr fee calculator takes your quoted percentage as an input, alongside any withdrawal fee and a tax reserve, and reports the take-home.

Common questions

How much does Upwork actually take from freelancers?

Since May 1, 2025, Upwork no longer uses its old 20%/10%/5% lifetime-billing tiers. It now charges a variable freelancer service fee between 0% and 15% per contract, set by Upwork’s own pricing system per client relationship and shown to you only when you send a proposal or receive an offer. There is no public formula this page — or anyone else’s — can compute for you: type in the percentage Upwork actually quoted you for this contract, and the page runs the arithmetic from there.

How much does Fiverr take from sellers?

Fiverr charges a flat 20% seller commission on every order, with no tiers and no volume discount, and it applies to tips as well as the order price. That figure is public and has not changed in years, so this page uses it as the default — you can override it if Fiverr changes its rate. See how much Fiverr actually takes for withdrawal fees, the escrow clearance period, and the tiered structure Fiverr retired in 2022.

Should I list a job on Upwork or Fiverr?

That depends on your own quoted Upwork fee for that client, since Upwork’s fee varies and Fiverr’s does not. Enter the same job price on both sides of this calculator with your actual quoted Upwork percentage, and it reports which platform nets you more for that specific job, by how much.

What price should I charge to take home a specific amount after fees?

Pick a platform and type a take-home goal, and the page solves backwards through that platform’s fee, its withdrawal fee, and your tax reserve to the job price that would leave you with that goal. It is the reverse of the main comparison: instead of pricing forward from a job price, it prices backward from what you want to keep.

How much should I set aside for taxes as an Upwork or Fiverr freelancer?

This page will not tell you a percentage — that depends on your filing status, state, total income, deductions, and quarterly-estimate schedule, and picking one for you would be a claim about what you owe. What it does is arithmetic once you tell it your own reserve percentage: it holds that share out of proceeds after the platform fee and withdrawal fee, on each platform, so you can see what a reserve actually does to a real job’s take-home. Ask a tax preparer for your percentage.

vs-checking-each-platforms-fee-page-sepa.text:
← Upwork vs. Fiverr Fee Calculator

This calculator vs. checking each platform's fee page separately

Fiverr's fee page states one number. Upwork's does not state a number at all any more — and reaching for the wrong one instead of your own quoted rate understates what a job actually pays.

What checking each platform's fee page by hand looks like

Fiverr's help pages are straightforward: a flat 20% seller commission, no tiers, applied to every order. Upwork's fee page is not the same kind of page any more. Since May 1, 2025 it does not publish a number — it explains that the freelancer service fee is set per contract, somewhere between 0% and 15%, by Upwork's own pricing system, and shown to you only at proposal time.

Checking both by hand means two tabs, the same job price typed in twice, and a subtraction done separately for each — and one of those two lookups was never going to hand you a rate to subtract with. The gap gets filled somehow, and the somehow is often the tiered 20%/10%/5% formula Upwork retired, because it is still repeated across older blog posts, forum answers, and calculators nobody has updated. See how much Upwork actually takes for what changed.

What this calculator does instead

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter one job price, your own Upwork-quoted percentage, Fiverr's rate (defaulted to its current 20%), and optional withdrawal fees and a tax reserve. It runs the same job price through both platforms' payout math at once and reports which nets more, by how much.

Checking each fee page separatelyWhat this calculator does instead
Fiverr's page gives a flat rate to subtract; Upwork's page gives a range and a policy, not a number. Takes your own quoted Upwork percentage as an input, so the arithmetic never depends on Upwork publishing one.
Nothing stops a lookup from reaching for the 20%/10%/5% tiered formula Upwork retired on May 1, 2025. Never assumes a formula on your behalf — there is none left to assume.
Requires typing the same job price into two separate lookups, once per platform. One job price, both platforms computed from it side by side.
Neither platform's own page nets an optional withdrawal fee or a tax reserve against the other's take-home. Nets both a withdrawal fee and a self-employment tax reserve out of each platform's payout, side by side.
Tells you what each platform charges, not which one nets you more for this job. Reports the gap and names whichever platform actually pays more for the same job price.

Same $3,000 job, two different fee lookups

Say an established-relationship freelancer is quoted a 5% Upwork service fee for a $3,000 job — assuming it is the first work billed to this client, the same assumption the retired tiers' own boundaries used. Run through this calculator's own arithmetic, that job nets $2,850: a 95% effective take-home.

Check Upwork's fee page instead, find no single rate to apply, and reach for the retired 20%-on-the-first-$500, 10%-up-to-$10,000, 5%-above formula: that computes a $350 fee and a $2,650 take-home — 88.3% effective. The retired formula understates this one job by $200, from a rate structure Upwork has not charged since May 2025. Price several jobs a month off that number and the shortfall compounds every time.

Common questions

Why not just check Upwork's fee page and Fiverr's fee page separately?

Because they answer different kinds of question. Fiverr's fee page states one number: a flat 20% seller commission, unchanged in years. Upwork's fee page does not state a number at all -- since May 1, 2025 it only explains that the freelancer service fee is set per contract, somewhere between 0% and 15%, by Upwork's own pricing system. Reading both pages still leaves you to open a second tab, retype the same job price, and do the subtraction yourself for each platform, and one of those two lookups was never going to hand you a number to subtract with in the first place.

What mistake does checking Upwork's fee page by hand risk?

Reaching for the tiered 20%/10%/5% formula Upwork retired on May 1, 2025. That formula is still repeated on older blog posts, forum answers, and other calculators that have not caught up, and unlike Fiverr's flat rate it looks exactly as authoritative as the number it replaced. A freelancer who checks Upwork's fee page, does not find a single rate, and pattern-matches to the old tiers they saw somewhere else ends up computing a fee Upwork no longer charges.

How big is that mistake in practice?

On a $3,000 job, assuming it is the first work billed to this client -- the same assumption the retired tiers' own boundaries used -- an established-relationship freelancer actually quoted 5% keeps $2,850, a 95% effective take-home. Applying the retired 20%-on-the-first-$500, 10%-up-to-$10,000, 5%-above formula instead computes a $350 fee and a $2,650 take-home, 88.3% effective -- $200 less than the freelancer will actually receive on this one job, from a formula that no longer applies to any Upwork contract.

Does this calculator know my exact Upwork fee?

No, and it does not guess with a formula either -- there is no public formula left to guess with. It takes the percentage Upwork already quoted you for this specific contract, shown to you at proposal time, and runs it through the same arithmetic as Fiverr's flat 20% for the same job price.

What does this calculator do that checking both pages separately does not?

It takes one job price, your quoted Upwork percentage, and Fiverr's rate, and reports both take-home figures side by side in one place, with an optional withdrawal fee and tax reserve netted out of each -- no second tab, no retyping the price a second time, and no formula to reach for since it never assumes one on your behalf.

Open the Upwork vs. Fiverr Fee Calculator to run your own quoted rate, or read how much Upwork actually takes for what changed and why there is no formula left to look up.

vs-tracking-it-in-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Upwork vs. Fiverr fee calculator

Upwork vs. Fiverr Fee Calculator vs. tracking it in a spreadsheet

A freelancer weighing the same job on both platforms usually ends up with a spreadsheet: a cell for Upwork's quoted fee, one for Fiverr's flat 20%, a withdrawal-fee line, and a tax-reserve percentage. Each formula is ordinary arithmetic. Keeping them right — especially remembering that Upwork retired its old 20%/10%/5% lifetime-billing tiers on 1 May 2025 in favor of a variable 0–15% fee quoted per contract — is the part that gets skipped when an older sheet or a generic fee-comparison page is reused for a new job.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every formula this calculator runs — each platform's cut, the flat withdrawal fee, the tax reserve, and the backward solve for a job price that hits a take-home goal. Building it means taking Upwork's fee as a manual per-contract input rather than a retired tiered formula, applying the withdrawal fee before the tax reserve in the same order on both sides, and getting the backward-solve algebra right rather than guessing a price and checking it.

This calculator keeps the job price, both platforms' net payouts, and the target take-home solve on one screen, already wired to the comparison tool. A shareable link carries the full scenario in the URL, and the Upwork fee explainer covers what changed in the May 2025 pricing update.

Worked example

A $1,200 job, Upwork's quoted fee at 8% for this client relationship, Fiverr's flat 20%, no withdrawal fee on Upwork, a $3 Fiverr withdrawal, and a 25% tax reserve on both:

After withdrawal fee$1,104.00$957.00
Tax reserve (25%)$276.00$239.25
Take-home$828.00 (69.0%)$717.75 (59.8%)

Upwork nets $110.25 more on this job — a gap that only shows up because both cuts are run through the same withdrawal-fee-then-tax-reserve order, the step a rebuilt spreadsheet formula most often gets backwards or drops.

Same freelancer, a smaller $500 job at Upwork's 15% quoted fee, wanting $400 take-home after the same 25% tax reserve: the calculator's backward solve says $627.45 is the price to charge on Upwork to hit that goal, a figure a guess-and-check spreadsheet cell usually takes several tries to land on.

This page names no specific product — it compares against the generic method of tracking these numbers in a spreadsheet, not a competing calculator. Common questions

Can a spreadsheet do this math instead?

Yes. The platform fee, the flat withdrawal fee, the tax reserve, and the backward solve for a target take-home are all ordinary arithmetic you can put in a spreadsheet. Getting there means encoding Upwork's fee as a manual input rather than a stale tiered formula, applying the withdrawal fee before the tax reserve on both platforms in the same order, and rebuilding the backward-solve formula correctly rather than just guessing a price and checking it.

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Keep the job price, both platforms' cuts, and the target take-home solve on one screen without re-deriving the formulas each time a rate changes. The easiest mistake to make by hand is reusing Upwork's old 20%/10%/5% lifetime-billing tiers, retired 1 May 2025 — a formula copied from an older sheet or a generic fee-comparison page will still use them. This calculator takes Upwork's fee as your own quoted figure every time, applies the withdrawal fee and tax reserve in the same order on both platforms, and produces a shareable link that carries the whole scenario instead of a file to keep in sync between two people.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when your situation has a wrinkle this calculator does not model — a multi-milestone contract with a different quoted Upwork fee per milestone, a currency conversion on top of the platform cut, or a fee structure from a plan or region this tool's inputs cannot represent. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields for pricing or evaluating one job on Upwork or Fiverr.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. A shareable link carries your numbers in the URL itself rather than sending them to a server, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your job price, fees, or tax reserve.
